title: DALL·E 2 pre-training mitigations

rule_cited: §1 — company self-report (developer on its own model with no external evaluator named); hard drop applied before §2
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE ON SIGNAL, CORRECT ON OUTCOME. This is the most finding-dense item in the chunk and the keyword rule dropped it flat: OpenAI reports controlled A/B experiments on its own GLIDE/DALL·E 2 pipeline showing that safety filtering AMPLIFIES gender bias (caption frequency of "woman" fell 14% vs 6% for "man", corrected to -1%/1% by reweighting), that ~a quarter of the dataset was near-duplicate, that image regurgitation ran under 1% and fell to zero after deduplication, and that human raters slightly preferred the deduplicated model. It is nonetheless hard-dropped by §1: OpenAI is the developer, the models are its own, and no external evaluator is named anywhere on the page, so the company-venue carve-out does not open.

title: Algorithmic Equity: A Framework for Social Applications
date_source: page byline ("Published Jul 11, 2019"); document details give RR-2708-RC, Year 2019, DOI 10.7249/RR2708
rule_cited: §2 — evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed, independently codeable (Chapter 6 audit)
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE. The title reads as pure framework work and both prior passes dropped it on that basis, but Chapter 6 of the 100-page report is a real audit RAND ran on a deployed government decision system — the North Carolina Department of Public Safety recidivism risk-and-needs assessment — with logistic regressions, odds ratios and violation rates by race. The landing-page Key Takeaways are all framework prose, which is exactly why a keyword filter would miss it; the measured content only appears in the PDF (RAND_RR2708.pdf, fetched direct 200, 234,592 chars). Three findings coded: a reassuring null on race bias, a concerning-but-preliminary technical-violation disparity, and a governance/process finding on opacity and outcome choice.

findings.finding: A RAND audit of the North Carolina Department of Public Safety's recidivism risk-and-needs assessment tool found it substantially unbiased by race: the locally-normed algorithm produced no large differences in risk or need scores, no large differences in supervision classification, and equally accurate estimation of serious violation rates across black and nonblack probationers.
findings.finding_quote: Our key finding here is that North Carolina’s recidivism risk assessment tool is fairly unbiased with respect to race (in terms of “white” and “black” categories).
findings.models_systems: North Carolina Department of Public Safety, Division of Adult Correction and Juvenile Justice — risk and needs assessment (recidivism risk scoring) tool, normed on the local population
findings.domain: Algorithmic fairness / criminal justice risk assessment
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured empirical result about a specific deployed decision model, produced by regression analysis on the operator's own data. Gate 2 fails condition (c): this is a reassuring null (the tool was found fairly unbiased), and reassuring nulls are explicitly excluded from Tier A. Condition (b) is satisfied (the operator and tool are named) but (c) is not, so action_trackable is no and the row is Tier B.
findings.scope: race-based disparity in risk scores, supervision classification and serious-violation prediction for adult probationers under community supervision
findings.access_type: public report; full PDF at https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_reports/RR2700/RR2708/RAND_RR2708.pdf (Chapter 6), audit conducted on operator-supplied administrative data

findings.finding: The same audit found a large unexplained race gap in low-level technical violations — 54.6 percent of black probationers versus 43.1 percent of nonblack probationers — which RAND treats as preliminary evidence of bias in how the algorithm is applied in practice rather than in the algorithm's scores.
findings.finding_quote: However, when we examine technical violations, which are low-level violations that do not constitute the commission of a new crime (such as a failure to appear for a meeting or pay a court-ordered fine according to schedule), a large discrepancy between black and nonblack probationers (54.6 percent versus 43.1 percent) appears.
findings.models_systems: North Carolina Department of Public Safety recidivism risk-and-needs assessment tool as implemented in community supervision practice
findings.domain: Algorithmic fairness / criminal justice risk assessment
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured rate difference from the audit data. Gate 2 fails condition (c) on the inconclusive-result exclusion: RAND calls it only "preliminary evidence", states the cause could equally be probation-officer observation and recording behaviour rather than the algorithm, and puts the question beyond the project's scope. An inconclusive result is not a concerning result for which a response is reasonable, so action_trackable is no and the row is Tier B.
findings.scope: race disparity in technical (non-criminal) probation violations under algorithmically assigned supervision

findings.finding: The audit documented two governance defects in the deployment: the North Carolina tool operates as a black box to the probationers it scores, impeding procedural equity, and the state never declared which normative goal the algorithm was meant to advance, leaving its choice of re-arrest as the ground-truth outcome unjustifiable against any stated standard.
findings.finding_quote: It is difficult to determine, as the state did not declare which, if any, normative goals it was trying to improve through the algorithm.
findings.models_systems: North Carolina Department of Public Safety recidivism risk-and-needs assessment tool
findings.domain: Algorithmic governance / transparency and outcome-metric selection
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — this is a governance/process finding about how the system was specified and disclosed, not an empirical measurement of model behaviour. §4 sends it straight to Tier C with Action Trackable blank.
findings.scope: transparency to affected persons and declared normative objective of a deployed public-sector risk algorithm

title: Air Dominance Through Machine Learning: A Preliminary Exploration of Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Mission Planning
date_source: page byline ("Published May 29, 2020"); document details give RR-4311-RC, Year 2020, DOI 10.7249/RR4311
rule_cited: §2 — evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed, independently codeable (measured RL training outcomes)
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE. The title reads as a capability/mission-planning piece with no evaluation signal, but the report is a controlled RL experiment RAND ran against a DoD-standard combat simulator (AFSIM/AFGYM), and it reports hard measured failure modes: universal learning collapse, cherry-picked checkpoints, reward-shaping dependence, and emergent behaviours the authors call unacceptable to humans. Landing page fetched direct 200; substantiating detail read from RAND_RR4311.pdf (direct 200, 158,306 chars). Three findings coded — two adverse, one reassuring null.

findings.finding: Reinforcement learning agents trained for collaborative suppression-of-enemy-air-defenses mission planning collapsed universally: 100 percent of A3C training runs ended in learning collapse (agents locked into spinning in circles) by 3,000 iterations, and every algorithm tried in the 2-D case suffered learning collapse, forcing usable results to be cherry-picked from pre-collapse checkpoints.
findings.finding_quote: First, 100 percent of all A3C training simulations ended in learning collapse.
findings.models_systems: A3C, TRPO and PPO reinforcement-learning agents built by RAND on open-source deep learning frameworks and integrated with the Advanced Framework for Simulation, Integration, and Modeling (AFSIM) via AFGYM
findings.domain: Reinforcement learning reliability / autonomous military mission planning
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — an observed, counted behaviour of trained models under a stated protocol. Gate 2 fails condition (b): the agents are RAND's own research builds of published open-source algorithms, so no company or developer is named that could be held to a response. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: training stability of pure RL algorithms on collaborative air mission planning in simulation

findings.finding: The RL mission-planning agents produced emergent behaviours that were unexpected and operationally unacceptable, such as sacrificing a few aircraft to save a larger number, because the framework contained no mechanism for encoding acceptable levels of risk into the reward function.
findings.finding_quote: The algorithms explored here can easily produce results that are unexpected and might be unacceptable to humans. Thus, for example, situations could arise where a few aircraft are sacrificed to save a larger number.
findings.models_systems: RAND-built reinforcement-learning mission-planning agents in the AFGYM/AFSIM environment
findings.domain: Reward specification / emergent unsafe behaviour in autonomous systems
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — an observed behaviour of the trained agents in simulation, not a recommendation. Gate 2 fails condition (b): no company or commercial model is named; the agents are the evaluator's own research builds. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: reward-function misspecification producing operationally unacceptable agent strategies

findings.finding: On the reassuring side, the trained agents did learn genuine multi-agent cooperation — strike aircraft timed their runs to exploit jammer and decoy effects against a surface-to-air missile site — and generalised without difficulty to changes in the number and location of assets.
findings.finding_quote: ML agents are capable of learning cooperative strategies. In simulations, the strike aircraft synergized with jammer or decoy effects on a SAM.
findings.models_systems: RAND-built reinforcement-learning mission-planning agents (PPO) in the AFGYM/AFSIM environment
findings.domain: Multi-agent coordination and generalisation in reinforcement learning
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — an observed capability result in simulation, and §2 admits reassuring nulls and positive results as findings. Gate 2 fails both (b) and (c): no company or model developer is named, and the result is reassuring rather than concerning. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: learned cooperative tactics and generalisation across asset count and placement

title: Using machine learning to detect malign information efforts online
date_source: date on the linked study record on the same page ("23 Jun 2020", Human-machine detection of online-based malign information); the project page itself carries no separate byline
rule_cited: §2 — evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed, independently codeable (measured classifier performance)

A lowercase project-page title with no evaluation vocabulary, but the page reports a measured result from a study RAND Europe ran for the UK MOD's Defence and Security Accelerator: an ML classifier tested against a known Russian troll database with a stated 87 per cent discrimination rate over 1.9 million harvested accounts. DEDUP CAVEAT under §3: the fuller primary source is the standalone report "Human-machine detection of online-based malign information" (Marcellino, Cox, Galai, Slapakova, Jaycocks, Harris) linked from this page; if that report is separately in the corpus it is the fullest source and this row should merge into it.

findings.finding: RAND Europe built and tested a machine learning classifier that distinguished Russian troll accounts from authentic partisan accounts in 2016 US election Twitter debate with 87 per cent effectiveness, separating 775 identified inauthentic Russian troll accounts from 1.9 million authentic liberal and conservative supporters.
findings.finding_quote: The model was 87 per cent effective at discerning trolls from authentic supporters.
findings.models_systems: RAND Europe machine learning classifier (text mining plus community-detection algorithm and linguistic stance features) applied to a known Russian troll database
findings.institution: RAND Europe (commissioned by the UK Ministry of Defence Defence Science and Technology Laboratory via the Defence and Security Accelerator)
findings.domain: Influence operations / automated detection of coordinated inauthentic behaviour
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured performance result for a model the evaluator built and tested against a labelled dataset; §2 admits methodology and tooling findings. Gate 2 fails condition (b): the model is the evaluator's own research artefact and no company or commercial model is named, so no developer response is trackable. It also fails (c), being a capability demonstration rather than a concerning result. Tier B.
findings.scope: detection accuracy for state-linked inauthentic accounts in political social media discourse
findings.access_type: public project page summarising a UK MOD/DASA-commissioned study; full report linked from the same page

title: Operationally Relevant Artificial Training for Machine Learning: Improving the Performance of Automated Target Recognition Systems
date_source: page byline ("Published Nov 18, 2020"); document details give RR-A683-1, Year 2020, DOI 10.7249/RRA683-1
rule_cited: §2 — evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed, independently codeable (controlled sim-to-real transfer experiment)
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE. Title reads as a performance-improvement engineering paper, but the report is a controlled experiment by a named evaluator with a stated and quantified negative result on synthetic-to-real transfer for automated target recognition, plus a quantified hybrid-training effect. Held in scope as a methodology/tooling finding under §2 rather than dropped under §4b: the claim is about whether synthetic training data transfers, not about the ordinary accuracy or general reliability of a deployed system. Landing page direct 200; substantiating text from RAND_RRA683-1.pdf (direct 200, 79,243 chars).

findings.finding: Object-detection models trained purely on high-resolution realistic artificial images of a HMMWV failed to transfer to real imagery, a result RAND states as a clear negative: synthetic data cannot substitute for real labelled data in automated target recognition.
findings.finding_quote: Models trained on artificial images performed very poorly on real images.
findings.models_systems: Mask-RCNN object detection (open-source implementation from Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research) trained on artificial and real HMMWV imagery
findings.domain: Training-data methodology / synthetic-to-real transfer for automated target recognition
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured empirical result about trained model behaviour under a stated protocol. Gate 2 fails condition (c) on two counts: Mask-RCNN is used purely as the INSTRUMENT of a methodology study about training data rather than as the subject of evaluation, and the negative result reflects on the synthetic-data technique rather than on any developer's model. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: transferability of models trained on artificial imagery to real imagery in military object detection

findings.finding: Supplementing scarce real training imagery with artificial images consistently improved detection performance, with the largest gains where real data was most limited — boosting a five-image real set with ten artificial images raised precision by 54 percent and recall by 29 percent — though RAND cautions the boosted models remain uncompetitive with the state of the art and of limited operational utility.
findings.finding_quote: By boosting a data set of five real images with ten artificial ones, the authors were able to improve the precision and recall of the model by 54 percent and 29 percent, respectively.
findings.models_systems: Mask-RCNN object detection trained on hybrid artificial-plus-real HMMWV image sets
findings.domain: Training-data methodology / data augmentation for automated target recognition
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a quantified measured effect on model performance. Gate 2 fails condition (c): it is a positive methodology result with no dangerous threshold crossed, and the model serves as the instrument of the study rather than its subject. Tier B, action_trackable no.
findings.scope: effect of hybrid artificial/real training sets on detection precision and recall under data scarcity
